_doc: Reel Reads audio recap scripts, one per book, ~2-2.5 min spoken. Written from general knowledge (and web sources for The Power Broker and Chasing the Flame, 26/10/2026). Order = ElevenLabs generation priority (Ambidex captures first). slug = audio/<slug>.mp3.

recaps.title: Power and Progress
recaps.author: Daron Acemoglu and Simon Johnson
recaps.text:
Power and Progress, by Daron Acemoglu and Simon Johnson. Here is the big idea in about two minutes.

We like to believe that new technology automatically makes everyone better off. Build a better machine, productivity rises, and sooner or later wages rise with it. Acemoglu and Johnson call this the productivity bandwagon, and they argue it is a myth, or at least a very conditional truth.

They walk through a thousand years of history to make the case. Medieval improvements in farming made monasteries and lords richer while peasants stayed poor. The early industrial revolution in Britain created enormous wealth, yet for several generations factory workers saw longer hours, worse health and flat real wages. Things only changed when workers organised, when the vote was extended and when new institutions forced the gains to be shared.

The lesson is that the direction of technology is a choice. Engineers and companies can design machines that replace workers, or machines that make workers more productive and create new tasks for them. Which one we get depends on who has power: who funds the research, who owns the systems and who has a voice in how they are used.

That brings the authors to artificial intelligence. Their worry is that much of today's AI is aimed at automation and surveillance, cutting labour costs and monitoring people, rather than at augmenting what humans can do. They call some of this so-so automation: technology that is good enough to replace a worker but not good enough to deliver big productivity gains. The result is lost jobs without much growth.

What do they propose? Redirect innovation toward tools that complement workers, rebalance the tax system so it stops favouring machines over people, strengthen worker voice and break up concentrated control over data and digital platforms.

The takeaway: progress is not something that happens to us. It is something a society steers. If you care about who benefits from AI, the question is not how powerful the models become, but who gets to decide what they are for.

recaps.title: War Is a Racket
recaps.author: Smedley D. Butler
recaps.text:
War Is a Racket, by Major General Smedley Butler. A short book with a blunt message, recapped in about two minutes.

Smedley Butler was one of the most decorated Marines in American history, a two-time Medal of Honor recipient who fought in the Philippines, China, Central America and the Caribbean. So when he published this short book in 1935, it landed hard. A career soldier was saying that war, as he had seen it, was a racket.

What does he mean by a racket? Something that is not what it seems to the majority of people. Only a small inside group knows what it is about, and it is conducted for the benefit of the very few at the expense of the very many.

Butler looks at the First World War and follows the money. He describes companies whose profits multiplied during the war: munitions makers, steel producers, shipbuilders and suppliers who sold the army everything from boots to mosquito nets, sometimes far more than it could ever use. Meanwhile the cost was paid by ordinary soldiers, in lives, wounds and broken minds, and by taxpayers who carried the debt for years.

He also turns the lens on his own career. Looking back, he says he spent much of his service as a muscle man for big business and for bankers, protecting American commercial interests abroad. It is a striking confession from someone inside the system.

His remedies are simple and radical. First, take the profit out of war: conscript capital and industry before you conscript young men, and pay executives and workers the same modest wage as soldiers. Second, let the people who would actually fight vote on whether to go to war. Third, limit the military to genuine defence of the homeland.

The lasting lesson goes beyond war. When a decision creates large gains for a few people and large costs for everyone else, look closely at who is pushing for it. Ask who profits, and who pays.

recaps.title: Just Mercy
recaps.author: Bryan Stevenson
recaps.text:
Just Mercy, by Bryan Stevenson. Here is the heart of the book in about two minutes.

Bryan Stevenson is a lawyer who founded the Equal Justice Initiative in Montgomery, Alabama. His work is defending people that the American justice system has largely given up on: the poor, the wrongly convicted, children sentenced as adults and people on death row.

The book is built around one case. Walter McMillian, a Black man in Monroeville, Alabama, was convicted of murdering a young white woman and sentenced to death, even though dozens of people could confirm he was at a family gathering when the crime happened. The case against him rested on testimony that was later shown to be coerced and false. Stevenson spent years fighting it, facing hostility and threats, until McMillian was finally exonerated and released after six years on death row.

Around that story, Stevenson weaves other cases: teenagers sentenced to die in prison, people with intellectual disabilities executed, women punished harshly for the circumstances of poverty. Together they show a pattern. The outcome of a case often depends less on what a person did than on whether they are poor, whether they are Black and whether anyone with resources is willing to fight for them.

Stevenson's central line is that each of us is more than the worst thing we have ever done. He argues that the true measure of a society is not how it treats the powerful, but how it treats the poor, the condemned and the incarcerated.

He also talks about proximity. You cannot understand a broken system from a distance. You have to get close to the people it affects, listen to them and let that change you.

And in the most personal passage, he admits his own brokenness. Doing this work, surrounded by suffering, he realises that mercy is not something the strong give to the weak. It is something we all need, because all of us are broken in some way.

The takeaway: justice is not just about guilt and innocence. It is about whether we are willing to see the full humanity of the people the system condemns.

recaps.title: The Billionaire's Vinegar
recaps.author: Benjamin Wallace
recaps.text:
The Billionaire's Vinegar, by Benjamin Wallace. A true story about wine, wealth and wanting to believe, in about two minutes.

In 1985, at Christie's in London, a single bottle of wine sold for a record price, roughly one hundred and fifty six thousand dollars. It was a 1787 Chateau Lafite, engraved with the initials Th.J. The story was irresistible: this was supposedly part of a cache of bottles that once belonged to Thomas Jefferson, the American founding father and famous wine lover, discovered behind a bricked-up wall in Paris.

The bottles came from one man, a charismatic German collector named Hardy Rodenstock, who was known for hosting lavish tastings of incredibly rare old wines. He never revealed exactly where the cellar was or how many bottles it held. The buyer of that first record bottle was the Forbes family, and other bottles from the same source later found their way into the hands of wealthy collectors.

One of those collectors was the American billionaire Bill Koch. When he tried to have his Jefferson bottles authenticated for a museum exhibition, the story began to crack. Jefferson experts found no record of these wines in his meticulous notes. Scientists tested the glass and the engraving, and the evidence suggested the initials were made with modern tools. Koch went to war, spending millions on investigators and lawsuits.

Wallace's point is not only about one possible fraud. It is about how the whole system wanted the story to be true. Auction houses earned commissions and headlines. Experts gained prestige from tasting legendary wines. Buyers paid for history, scarcity and the feeling of owning something unique. Almost nobody had an incentive to ask hard questions.

That is why the book matters well beyond wine. Whenever an asset is rare, glamorous and comes with a great story, due diligence quietly switches off. The lesson for any deal, from fine wine to a startup acquisition: the better the story, the harder you should check the provenance.

recaps.title: The Power Broker
recaps.author: Robert A. Caro
recaps.text:
The Power Broker, by Robert Caro. A thirteen-hundred-page masterpiece about power, recapped in about two minutes.

Published in 1974 and winner of the Pulitzer Prize, The Power Broker is the biography of Robert Moses, the man who shaped modern New York more than any mayor or governor. He built bridges like the Triborough, parkways, expressways, beaches, parks and housing projects. Yet he was never elected to anything. He held appointed positions, sometimes many at once, and for decades he had more power than the elected officials who were supposed to oversee him.

Caro's story has two halves. In the first, Moses is an idealistic young reformer who wants to build parks and beaches for ordinary people, but he gets nowhere because he lacks power. So he learns how to get it. He drafts legislation himself, filling it with clauses only he understands. He masters the public authority, a body that could issue bonds and collect tolls. Bridge tolls gave him a stream of money that no mayor controlled, and with money came contracts, jobs and loyalty from banks, unions and politicians.

In the second half, the cost appears. Caro shows how Moses ran highways straight through neighbourhoods, evicting huge numbers of people, many of them poor and many of them Black or Puerto Rican, and destroying communities like East Tremont for the Cross Bronx Expressway. He favoured cars over public transit, and the city lived with those choices for generations. The idealist had become a man who used power for its own sake.

Caro's broader insight is that power does not always corrupt, but it always reveals. Once people have enough of it, you finally see what they really wanted to do all along.

The takeaways: real power often sits in unelected, unglamorous places, such as authorities, budgets and fine print. Control over an independent source of money is control over everything else. And any system that lets one person escape accountability will eventually show you the dark side of their vision.

recaps.title: Chasing the Flame
recaps.author: Samantha Power
recaps.text:
Chasing the Flame, by Samantha Power. The life of a remarkable diplomat, in about two minutes.

Sergio Vieira de Mello was a Brazilian who spent over three decades at the United Nations. Samantha Power, drawing on hundreds of interviews, follows him through almost every major crisis of his era. He worked with refugees in Bangladesh and Lebanon, negotiated with the Khmer Rouge to bring Cambodian refugees home, and served in Bosnia and Kosovo.

His biggest test came in East Timor. After the territory voted for independence from Indonesia in 1999 and was left burning, the UN put Vieira de Mello in charge. For more than two years he effectively ran the country, building a government almost from scratch until East Timor became independent. It was a quasi-colonial role, and Power shows both his skill and his blind spots: he learned that outsiders governing a people, however well meaning, need local legitimacy, and he shifted toward sharing power with Timorese leaders.

In 2002 he became the UN High Commissioner for Human Rights. Then, in 2003, he was sent to Baghdad after the American invasion of Iraq. In August that year a bomb struck the UN headquarters at the Canal Hotel. He was trapped in the rubble and died, along with twenty one others, in one of the deadliest attacks the UN has ever suffered.

What makes the book more than a biography is its portrait of pragmatism. Vieira de Mello was charming and flexible. He was willing to talk to anyone, including people with blood on their hands, if it moved things forward. Power admires that, while also showing where his compromises failed, and how the gap between the UN's ideals and its real power kept trapping him.

The takeaways: idealism without pragmatism achieves little, but pragmatism without principles loses its way. Legitimacy comes from the people you serve, not from your mandate. And the hardest leadership happens in the space between what you believe and what you can actually get done.

recaps.title: Power
recaps.author: Jeffrey Pfeffer
recaps.text:
Power: Why Some People Have It and Others Don't, by Jeffrey Pfeffer. In about two minutes.

Jeffrey Pfeffer teaches at Stanford's business school, and this book is a deliberate antidote to the comforting story most of us are told: work hard, do great work, be nice, and you will be rewarded. Pfeffer's research says that story is mostly wrong. Performance matters less than we think for who gets promoted, who keeps their job and who gets paid more. What matters a great deal is power.

So where does power come from? Partly from personal qualities. Pfeffer points to ambition, energy, focus, self-knowledge, confidence, empathy for others' points of view and a tolerance for conflict. You do not need all of them, but people who build power usually have several.

It also comes from what you do. Get noticed: your boss is busy and does not automatically see your work, so make it visible. Ask for things: people are far more willing to help than we expect, and most of us ask too rarely. Choose where you start: departments and roles that control critical resources or problems give you a platform. Build a network deliberately, especially ties that bridge otherwise separate groups, because the person in the middle controls the flow of information.

Pfeffer also talks about how you show up. Acting and speaking with power, being calm, direct and decisive rather than hesitant and apologetic, shapes how others see you. Anger and confidence can be more persuasive than modesty. And reputation tends to become self-fulfilling.

He is honest about the costs too: visibility, scrutiny, loss of freedom, the time and energy it takes, and the risk of becoming overconfident once you have power. Many powerful people lose it because they stop paying attention.

The takeaway: waiting to be recognised is a strategy, and usually a losing one. If you want to make an impact inside an organisation, you have to understand power and build it on purpose.

recaps.title: The Education of an Idealist
recaps.author: Samantha Power
recaps.text:
The Education of an Idealist, by Samantha Power. A memoir, recapped in about two minutes.

Samantha Power was born in Ireland, moved to the United States as a child, and in her twenties became a war correspondent in Bosnia. What she saw there, including the failure of the world to stop ethnic cleansing, shaped everything that came after. She wrote a Pulitzer Prize winning book about genocide and how the United States repeatedly failed to respond to it.

Then she did something unusual for a critic. She went inside. She worked for Barack Obama when he was a senator, joined his White House on the National Security Council, and later became the US Ambassador to the United Nations.

The memoir is about what happens to ideals inside a government. Power describes real wins: building coalitions to fight the Ebola outbreak in West Africa, pushing for the release of political prisoners and championing individual cases that might otherwise have been forgotten. She also faces the hardest failure of her time in office, Syria, where the administration did not intervene as the civil war killed hundreds of thousands of people. She does not hide from that, and she reflects openly on what she could and could not change.

The book is also personal and funny. She writes about anxiety, about balancing motherhood with a punishing job, about her family and about the feeling of being an outsider in rooms of power.

Her central lesson is that idealism is not a pose you hold from the sidelines. It is a practice. Inside institutions, progress comes from persistence, coalitions, compromise and small concrete acts for real people, even when the big picture looks bleak. Cynicism is easy and it changes nothing.

The takeaway: if you want to change an institution, you have to be willing to stay in the room, accept imperfect wins and keep going.

recaps.title: Blue Ocean Strategy
recaps.author: W. Chan Kim and Renee Mauborgne
recaps.text:
Blue Ocean Strategy, by W. Chan Kim and Renee Mauborgne of INSEAD. In about two minutes.

Most companies compete in what the authors call red oceans: existing markets where everyone fights over the same customers with the same offer. Competition becomes a bloody fight over price and features, and profits shrink.

Blue oceans are the opposite: uncontested market space where demand is created rather than fought over, and competition becomes irrelevant. The classic example is Cirque du Soleil. The circus industry was in decline, with star performers and animal acts making it expensive. Cirque removed the animals and the stars, kept the tent, the clowns and the acrobatics, and added theatre, story and artistic music. It created a new form of entertainment and attracted adults and corporate clients who would never buy a circus ticket.

The key concept is value innovation: pursuing differentiation and low cost at the same time, rather than trading one off against the other. To do it, the authors offer the four actions framework. Ask which factors the industry takes for granted that you can eliminate. Which factors you can reduce well below the standard. Which you can raise well above it. And which new factors you can create that the industry has never offered.

They also use the strategy canvas, a simple chart of how competitors score on each factor. If your line looks just like everyone else's, you are in a red ocean. A blue ocean strategy has a clearly different shape, with focus, divergence and a compelling tagline.

Finally, they urge you to look at noncustomers: the people who refuse your industry, or barely use it. Understanding why they stay away often reveals the biggest opportunity.

The takeaway: stop benchmarking the competition. Redefine the problem, create new demand and make the competition irrelevant.

recaps.title: The Lean Startup
recaps.author: Eric Ries
recaps.text:
The Lean Startup, by Eric Ries. In about two minutes.

Eric Ries starts from a painful observation: most startups do not fail because they cannot build their product. They fail because they build something nobody wants, and they discover it only after spending all their time and money.

His answer is to treat a startup as an experiment. A startup, he says, is a human institution designed to create a new product or service under conditions of extreme uncertainty. Under that uncertainty, a detailed five-year plan is fiction. What you need is a fast way to learn.

That way is the build, measure, learn loop. Build a minimum viable product, the smallest thing that lets you test your riskiest assumption with real customers. Measure how they actually behave, not what they say. Learn whether your assumption was right, and feed that into the next version. The goal is to get through the loop as quickly as possible.

The unit of progress is validated learning. Shipping features, writing code and raising money feel like progress, but they are not, unless they teach you something true about what customers want. Ries warns against vanity metrics, such as total sign-ups that only go up, and favours actionable metrics, like cohort conversion rates, that show cause and effect.

At some point the data forces a decision: persevere or pivot. A pivot is a structured change of course that keeps what you have learned, such as targeting a different customer segment or turning one feature into the whole product.

Ries also argues that this applies inside big companies, not just garages. Any team building something new under uncertainty is a startup, and it needs protected space and different accountability.

The takeaway: stop perfecting in private. Get something real in front of customers early, measure honestly and let validated learning decide what you build next.

recaps.title: The Innovator's Dilemma
recaps.author: Clayton Christensen
recaps.text:
The Innovator's Dilemma, by Clayton Christensen. In about two minutes.

Christensen asked a puzzling question: why do great, well managed companies, the ones that listen to customers and invest in better products, so often lose their markets to small newcomers?

His answer is that they fail precisely because they do everything right. He distinguishes two kinds of innovation. Sustaining innovations make existing products better for existing customers: faster, more powerful, more premium. Incumbents are excellent at these. Disruptive innovations are different. They start out worse on the dimensions mainstream customers care about, but they are cheaper, simpler, smaller or more convenient, and they appeal to new or less demanding customers.

His famous study is the disk drive industry. Each new, smaller drive size was first rejected by the leading firms' best customers, because it had less capacity. So the leaders ignored it. Newcomers sold it into new markets, improved it rapidly and eventually it became good enough for the mainstream. By then the incumbents were too late, and a whole generation of leaders fell.

Why does this happen? Because a rational incumbent allocates resources to its most profitable customers and its biggest markets. A small, low margin, uncertain market looks unattractive. The processes and values that make a company successful are exactly the ones that make it reject disruption.

Christensen's prescription is to give a disruptive technology to an independent organisation that is small enough to get excited about small wins, has its own cost structure and serves the customers who actually want the new thing. Plan for learning, not for precise forecasts, because nobody can size a market that does not exist yet.

The takeaway: the discipline that made you win can blind you to what comes next. Watch the cheap, worse product that your best customers dismiss. It may be the future.

recaps.title: Thinking, Fast and Slow
recaps.author: Daniel Kahneman
recaps.text:
Thinking, Fast and Slow, by Daniel Kahneman. In about two minutes.

Kahneman, a psychologist who won the Nobel Prize in economics, describes the mind as two systems. System one is fast, automatic, intuitive and emotional. It reads faces, finishes sentences and makes snap judgements effortlessly. System two is slow, deliberate and effortful. It does long division, checks arguments and resists temptation. System two thinks it is in charge, but most of the time it lazily accepts what system one suggests.

That is efficient, but it produces predictable errors, which Kahneman and his partner Amos Tversky catalogued for decades. A few to remember. Anchoring: an arbitrary number shapes your estimate, which is why first offers in negotiations matter. Availability: you judge how likely something is by how easily examples come to mind, so vivid news distorts your sense of risk. What you see is all there is: system one builds a confident story from whatever information it has, and ignores what is missing. Overconfidence and the planning fallacy: we consistently underestimate how long and how much projects will cost.

The second big contribution is prospect theory. People do not evaluate outcomes in absolute terms but as gains and losses relative to a reference point, and losses hurt roughly twice as much as equivalent gains feel good. This loss aversion explains why people hold losing investments too long and resist change. Framing matters too: the same choice described as lives saved or lives lost produces different decisions.

Kahneman also separates the experiencing self from the remembering self. We remember experiences by their peak and their end, not their duration.

What can you do about it? You cannot switch system one off. But you can recognise situations where errors are likely, slow down, use checklists, look for base rates and ask others to challenge your story.

The takeaway: a confident snap judgement is often a biased one. Know which system is driving.

recaps.title: The Goal
recaps.author: Eliyahu Goldratt
recaps.text:
The Goal, by Eliyahu Goldratt. A business novel about operations, in about two minutes.

The hero is Alex Rogo, a plant manager whose factory is late on orders, losing money and three months away from being closed. Through a series of conversations with his old physics teacher, Jonah, he discovers a new way to think about his plant.

First, what is the goal? Not efficiency, not keeping machines busy, not cost cutting. The goal of a business is to make money, now and in the future. Goldratt measures that with three simple measures: throughput, the rate at which the system generates money through sales; inventory, the money tied up in things you intend to sell; and operating expense, the money spent turning inventory into throughput.

The central insight comes on a scout hike. Alex notices that the whole troop can only move as fast as the slowest boy, Herbie. Every system has a constraint, a bottleneck, that limits its total output. An hour lost at the bottleneck is an hour lost for the entire system. An hour saved anywhere else is a mirage.

This leads to the five focusing steps of the theory of constraints. Identify the constraint. Exploit it, so it never sits idle or works on the wrong thing. Subordinate everything else to it, so other steps work at its pace instead of piling up inventory. Elevate it, by adding capacity if needed. And when the constraint moves, repeat, without letting inertia become the new constraint.

Alex applies this, putting the slowest boy at the front of the hike and, in the plant, prioritising the bottleneck machines. Inventory falls, orders ship on time and the plant is saved.

The takeaway: a system is only as fast as its slowest step. Before you improve anything, find the constraint, because effort spent elsewhere produces zero real throughput.

recaps.title: The Black Swan
recaps.author: Nassim Nicholas Taleb
recaps.text:
The Black Swan, by Nassim Nicholas Taleb. In about two minutes.

For centuries Europeans believed all swans were white, because every swan they had ever seen was white. Then black swans were found in Australia, and a single observation overturned a belief built on millions. Taleb uses this to name a kind of event: a black swan is rare, has an extreme impact and is explained only after the fact, as if it had been predictable.

His claim is that history, markets and our own lives are shaped mostly by black swans, not by the average days we study. The internet, the First World War, the financial crisis: none were forecast, and all changed everything. Yet we keep building models that assume the future will look like the past.

Taleb explains why we miss them. The narrative fallacy: we love tidy stories, so we invent causes after events. Silent evidence: we study the winners and never see the graveyard of failures. And the turkey problem: a turkey is fed every day for a thousand days, and its confidence grows daily, right up until the day before Thanksgiving.

He distinguishes two worlds. Mediocristan is where things are bounded, like height or weight; no single observation changes the average much. Extremistan is where one observation can dominate everything, like wealth, book sales or market crashes. Many of our tools, such as the bell curve, belong to Mediocristan but get applied to Extremistan, which is dangerous.

So what should you do? Stop trying to predict the unpredictable. Instead, focus on exposure. Protect yourself against negative black swans with redundancy and by avoiding ruin. Expose yourself to positive ones by keeping many small bets with limited downside and huge potential upside, a barbell approach.

The takeaway: the rare event is not the exception, it is the story. Build for a world where the unimaginable happens.

recaps.title: Against the Gods
recaps.author: Peter L. Bernstein
recaps.text:
Against the Gods: The Remarkable Story of Risk, by Peter Bernstein. In about two minutes.

Bernstein argues that the idea of risk, the belief that the future is not simply the whim of the gods but something we can measure and manage, is what separates the modern world from the past. His book is a history of how humanity learned to do that.

The story starts with numbers. The adoption of Hindu-Arabic numerals in Europe made calculation possible. Then, in the Renaissance, gamblers asked mathematicians how to split the stakes of an unfinished game. Blaise Pascal and Pierre de Fermat answered in letters, founding probability theory.

From there the cast grows. Jacob Bernoulli showed that with enough observations, averages become reliable, the law of large numbers. Daniel Bernoulli introduced utility: the value of money depends on how much you already have, which is why people buy insurance. Abraham de Moivre and Carl Friedrich Gauss described the bell curve. Francis Galton discovered regression to the mean, the tendency of extreme results to be followed by more ordinary ones. Thomas Bayes showed how to update beliefs with new evidence.

These ideas built insurance, through Lloyd's coffee house in London, and later modern finance. Harry Markowitz showed that diversification reduces risk without necessarily sacrificing return, which led to portfolio theory.

But Bernstein ends with caution. Daniel Kahneman and Amos Tversky showed that real people do not behave like the rational calculators in the models. And numbers can create false confidence: models built on the past can fail when the future is truly different, a theme Keynes raised long before.

The takeaway: mastering risk means using probability without worshipping it. Measure what you can, diversify, update with evidence, and remember that the models are tools, not prophecies.

recaps.title: Freakonomics
recaps.author: Steven Levitt and Stephen Dubner
recaps.text:
Freakonomics, by economist Steven Levitt and journalist Stephen Dubner. In about two minutes.

The book's premise is that economics is really the study of incentives, and that with good data you can use it to explain almost anything, including things that seem to have nothing to do with money.

Incentives come in three flavours, economic, social and moral, and people respond to all of them, often in ways the designer never intended. The famous example is an Israeli day care centre that introduced a small fine for parents who picked up their children late. Late pickups went up. The fine replaced a moral incentive, guilt, with a cheap price, and parents happily paid it.

Levitt then hunts for hidden cheating. Using test score data, he showed that some Chicago school teachers were changing their students' answers when their jobs depended on results. Looking at sumo wrestling records, he found wrestlers on the edge of an important threshold won suspiciously often against opponents with nothing at stake.

Another chapter asks why many drug dealers live with their mothers. Using a gang's financial records, the authors show the business is like a franchise: a few at the top earn a lot, while foot soldiers earn very little and take enormous risks, hoping to win the tournament for the top jobs.

The most controversial claim links the legalisation of abortion in the United States in the 1970s to the drop in crime in the 1990s, arguing that fewer unwanted children grew up in the circumstances that predict crime. It remains debated.

Along the way they show the gap between conventional wisdom and data, and how experts, from estate agents to doctors, can use information advantages for their own benefit.

The takeaway: if behaviour looks irrational, you probably have not found the real incentive yet. Look at the data, not the story people tell.

recaps.title: The Art of Strategy
recaps.author: Avinash Dixit and Barry Nalebuff
recaps.text:
The Art of Strategy, by Avinash Dixit and Barry Nalebuff. Game theory for everyday life, in about two minutes.

Game theory is the science of strategic thinking: situations where your best move depends on what others do, and theirs depends on you. The authors show it applies to business, negotiation, politics and even family life.

The first rule: look forward and reason backward. In games where moves happen in sequence, picture the end of the game, work out what each player will do at the last step, then roll back to your choice today. It is how chess players and good negotiators think.

When players move at the same time, you need to put yourself in the other side's shoes. If you have a dominant strategy, one that is best whatever they do, use it. If not, eliminate their dominated options and look for an equilibrium, where nobody wants to change their move given what the others are doing. That is the Nash equilibrium.

The prisoners' dilemma explains why rational individuals end up worse off together: each has an incentive to cheat, so cooperation collapses, as in price wars. Cooperation becomes possible when the game repeats. Strategies like tit for tat, cooperate first then mirror the other player, can sustain it.

The authors also cover commitment and credibility. A threat or promise only works if the other side believes you will carry it out, so strategists burn bridges, sign contracts or build reputations to make commitments credible. Sometimes limiting your own options makes you stronger.

They discuss mixing strategies to stay unpredictable, like a penalty taker in football, and signalling and screening, how people reveal or hide information, as with education signalling ability.

The takeaway: great strategists think about the other player's next moves, not just their own. Anticipate, reason backward and make your commitments credible.

recaps.title: Effectuation
recaps.author: Saras Sarasvathy
recaps.text:
Effectuation, by Saras Sarasvathy. How expert entrepreneurs actually think, in about two minutes.

Sarasvathy studied experienced founders, people who had built companies successfully several times, and gave them a business problem to think through out loud. She expected classic planning: set a goal, research the market, find the resources. Instead she found a different logic, which she called effectuation.

Causal thinking starts with a goal and asks how to achieve it. Effectual thinking starts with what you have and asks what you could do with it. Like a cook who opens the fridge and decides what to make, instead of choosing a recipe and shopping for it.

She describes five principles. The bird in hand: start with your means, who you are, what you know and whom you know. Affordable loss: instead of chasing the biggest expected return, decide what you can afford to lose, and act within it, which makes action possible even when the future is unknowable. The crazy quilt: build partnerships with people who commit early, and let their commitments shape what the venture becomes, rather than doing competitive analysis first. Lemonade: treat surprises as opportunities, not as deviations from a plan. And the pilot in the plane: the future is not something to predict but something to make, through the actions of you and your partners.

The underlying idea is that in truly new markets, prediction is impossible, so control matters more than forecasting. Goals emerge from action and from the people who join you.

This does not mean planning is useless. In established markets with good data, causal reasoning works. But at the very start of something new, effectuation is how experts move.

The takeaway: you do not need the perfect plan. Start with what you have, risk only what you can afford to lose, bring in committed partners and take the next affordable step.
